So why is it so hard to search these media types together in one query?
The main problem is that searching across multiple types of media requires one of two compromises.
One option is to combine multiple pipelines with a separate embedding model and a separate index
for each one. With this approach, the system needs one model for text, another for vision, and a third
for audio. Each produces its own embeddings stored in its own index. And when a user performs
a search, the system runs queries against each index separately and gets back separate results
sets. It's a lot of infrastructure and maintenance, and the results might still be mediocre because you need to
combine these results from separate searches at the ranking stage, somehow comparing apples
to oranges from separate embedding spaces. Now the second option is to use a multi-model
embedding model. The problem with this approach typically is that the models tend to be quite massive.
We're talking multiple billions of parameters with some as big as 7 billion parameters or even
larger. This means the models can be slow and expensive to run. Some frontier models with
these multi-model capabilities are close weight, which means you don't really know what's in
inside and you can't run them locally. The new Gena V5 Omni models solve all of these
as compact Omni modality models that handle text, images, audio and video, all mapped into a single
embedding space. The V5 Omni small is about 1.66 billion priors with all the extensions loaded,
and the Nano is about 1 billion parameters. Their compact size makes them very efficient,
with the Nano model in particular able to even run on commodity hardware. The model's efficiency,
see goes beyond the top line size. With the Omni models, each media encoder is a separate module
loaded at runtime. If you only need image and video search, the audio encoder is not loaded. If
you only need audio, the same thing, the vision module is skipped. So you're not wasting resources
on parts of the model that's not used. They call this dynamic weight loading. This is thanks to the
general architecture of the model, which the Gina team's paper calls geometry preserving embeddings via
locked online towers, or gelato. In other words, the V5-ovni models are composed of discrete
models. It takes encoders that were already trained inside other models and bolts the monster V5
text backbone without retraining any of them. In fact, the only new training is the tiny projector layers
that sit between each encoder and the text model, representing just 0.35% of the total
model weights. That's another reason that this model is so compact. But size means very little, of course,
